utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Would the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djukanovic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you commence your evidence, Mr. Djukanovic, I must draw your attention to a certain Rule that we have here at the International Tribunal, that is, Rule 90(E) of Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Under this Rule you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecution, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of your guilt in a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question, but in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled under such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, Mr. Djukanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Djukanovic.

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to speak slowly when you answer my questions and also to make a little pause after my question before you start providing your answers. This will allow the interpreters to interpret correctly.

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you provide a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did provide a statement to your Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D7971.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at the screen. Do you see a statement on the screen?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That is my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you read the statement and did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I read it fully and I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we go to the last page. Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is my signature, and I accept this statement as my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement faithfully reflect what you said to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I personally simplified something. I referred to all of the people there as volunteers, but this is not a good term. I believe that this is a mistake that I made. All the volunteers who came and put themselves under the command of the JNA were good fighters, and they fought with us. I'm saying this to make sure that these people are separated from paramilitaries. And "paramilitaries" is the term that I should have used for some of the formations that arrived in Bratunac at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you apply that correction to a particular paragraph or is that something that applies across the board and you will explain it during your live testimony?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Wherever I used the term "volunteer," if it is in a negative context I would like to correct it. I can't see exactly where I used that term. I believe that there are 64 paragraphs here. That will take a lot of time to correct. However, whenever I use the term "volunteers," I would like to change it and correct it if I may insist on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In addition to that, is there anything else in the statement would you -- that you would like to correct or is everything as you stated?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Everything is there that I stated. I stated this as well. I used the term "volunteers." In the meantime I had another thought and I decided to correct that. The person who took my statement made a very clear record of what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions to you today, would your answers be the same in essence?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they would be absolutely the same. Only if either you or the Trial Chamber or somebody else asked me to clarify things, then I could probably expand on the statement which is just a short summary of the events. I'm sure that I would have more to save -- say on the events if need be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this statement pursuant to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We also have one associated exhibit, and we would ask that it be added to our 65 ter list as it was a late addition to the witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Edgerton. Do you have any objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I was actually having a look at that document, thinking that there's insufficient foundation for the admission of that document as an associated exhibit, and perhaps Dr. Karadzic could address the circumstances within which the witness saw the document in the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do you have any difficulty with that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Save for the fact that we are wasting time, there is nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the view that paragraph 5 of this statement is irrelevant or unnecessary, so it can be redacted. With that redaction, we'll admit the Rule 92 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3194, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, just to be clear, do you want that document led live?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm now going to read a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. The Chamber has no difficulty if Mr. Karadzic addresses the issue raised by Ms. Edgerton, and then after we admit it. So we'll admit the associated exhibit as well. Shall we give the number for that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 1D7024 will be Exhibit D3195.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, would you mind if we left that to Ms. Edgerton to address if she thinks it's important?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I would like Mr. Karadzic to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. With all due respect to your decision with regard to paragraph 5, I thought that it would be good to know where all -- when all the tension started. They didn't start with the emergence of the SDS. I respect your decision, however, and in that I think that we are losing one important part of a whole. Now I'm going to read Mr. Djukanovic's summary statement in English. [In English] Rodoljub Djukanovic was born on 19th of July, 1952, in Kravica, Bratunac. He was a member of the Crisis Staff of Bratunac municipality in 1992, and president of the Bratunac Executive Committee. After the multi-party elections, a multi-party municipal government was formed in Bratunac. Nijaz Dubicic was elected president of the Municipal Assembly. At the end of August 1991, a crowd of Muslims attacked a military police unit which was saved by the police who intervened. The military policemen were forced to fire shots in the air to disperse the crowd. All sorts of swear words and insults were hurled in the army -- at the army and the Serbs. The following day, the Muslims around Bratunac continued to yell and provoke the Serbs. At the entrance of the Hotel Fontana, the Muslims physically attacked a man only because he was a Serb and from Kravica. At around April 1992, Rodoljub Djukanovic attended a meeting in Bratunac. On the return from the meeting, Nijaz told him that he wanted to take out of Bratunac all Muslims wishing to go to Tuzla and asking to secure escort for them so that they would not be mistreated at police check-points. Police patrols were provided. On 2nd of May, 1992, in Hranca, Muslims attacked a JNA military column that was withdrawing from Croatia through Central Bosnia. Rodoljub Djukanovic heard some people were killed and wounded. The next day he learned that some people had been brought from Hranca and placed in the hangar of the Vuk Karadzic Elementary School in Bratunac. He was not much involved in it. Later, he was informed that some bodies were found near the River Drina and some people were believed to be killed in the hangar. On May 8, 1992, Goran Zekic, chairman of the Srebrenica SDS Municipal Board and esteemed judge, was killed in a Muslim ambush just outside Srebrenica. This caused panic among the Serbs there. Then Miroslav Deronjic informed them that they should only disarm the Muslims in Glogova in order to ensure the safety of the Bratunac. He emphasised that the Crisis Staff had decided to disarm Glogova but not to kill any civilians. After the incident in Glogova, he learned that some Muslims from Suha and Seliste were being brought to the football stadium, which was guarded by armed volunteers in Bratunac. He went to the police station and asked about the situation. The chief of the SJB, Milutin Milosevic, told him that he did not know what was happening in the stadium because he received an order not to interfere with the work of the army/military police. Because the volunteers were causing them problems in Bratunac, paramilitaries were causing them problems in Bratunac, after some discussions in a meeting the Crisis Staff decided to throw them out of Bratunac. Later, he learned that the Muslims at the stadium that day had been transferred to the hangar of the primary school. Then he was informed that killings were taken place and dead bodies were found there. Right after this, the Crisis Staff decided that the people in the hangar must be saved and moved to Pale. In the second half of May 1992, the Serbian villages of Mratinci and Lipenovici were attacked, some civilians were killed and wounded, houses and property were destroyed. On 29th of May, 1992, in Sandici, the Muslim armed forces ambushed a group of officers from Bratunac Territorial Defence and Milutin Milosevic who were on their way to Milici. The chief of the police was seized. The Muslims then began to launch selective attacks on all Serbian villages in Bratunac and Srebrenica. It was mostly civilians that were killed in these villages. The most vicious massacres carried out by the Muslims were the ones that took place in Bjelovac and Sikiric on 14th of December, 1992, and in Kravica on the 7th of January, 1993, which was Christian Orthodox Christmas. At the municipal government they never received any orders from President Karadzic regarding the undertaking of any actions. They received one order in March 1993 when President Karadzic personally ordered that a humanitarian convoy carrying food for Srebrenica must be let through.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djukanovic, in paragraph 54 you mention a document which was shown to you. Unfortunately, paragraph 5 has been omitted. It speaks about the long history of tensions between the ethnic groups in Bratunac. Can you tell us what you knew about the arming and preparations for the war of the Muslim ethnic community in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Since I was the president of the Executive Board, sometimes I found reports from the SDB on my desk. We could learn from those reports that the Muslims were being guard [as interpreted] from Sandzak and from Sarajevo, and that those incidents were not sporadic. This was a large-scale exercise. This caused concern among us Serbs. It caused fear among the people, so the Serbs started arming themselves. They started buying weapons. It says here in this paragraph that we received an official note from the Tuzla DB. There is a list of persons there who are under threat, who could be killed. Moreover, it says in that note who were the highest profile individuals. At that moment, all that was very bad, because one could lose their life as a result of that. Since I occupied a position that was given to the Serbs, I was also on that list for liquidation. It soon proved to be true, because an unknown perpetrator opened fire on me. He shot at me. His name was Dautovic. So he was not unknown. He shot at me without any reason at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please can you slow down.

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I may have been speaking too fast. That person Dautovic shot at me near the bus-stop. He didn't have a reason to do that. I didn't know him. He was an 18-year-old lad. Luckily enough, he missed me, and I'm still here to tell the tale.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D7024.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the document to be displayed, could you please tell us who is in charge of the CSB in Tuzla in September 1991? Which ethnic group was a majority there?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: There was a Muslim majority there, and I believe that the chief of the CSB was a person called Saric, also Muslim. I believe that he hailed from Kladanj. I believe that this is a very realistic picture of the situation as it was in Bratunac at the time. There are some situations that I did not agree with. It says here that some person I personally know, Jovan Nikolic, myself, Goran Zekic, Miroslav Deronjic and I distributed people -- distributed weapons to people. I guarantee you that I never gave any weapons to anybody. I was not involved in the distribution of weapons. I suppose that this is just rumours that came from all sorts of people. This is the only thing that I don't agree with. Everything else is more or less a true reflection of the real situation as it was in Bratunac at the time, the state of chaos that reigned supreme and the foreboding of what would happen after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what were the forms of legal and illegal arming of the Serbs in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: The legal forms of arming could be seen at the end of 1991. Alija Delimustafic, who was the minister of the interior, and he issued an order to mobilise the reserve force of the police. This is what you call it in the police jargon. The ethnic composition reflected the ethnic composition of the population in Bratunac. There were 64 per cent of Muslims, 34 of Serbs, and the rest were others. I believe that there were some Roma and several Croats, and that's how the weapons were distributed. I believe that several hundred police officers were mobilised from the reserve force. Muslims received 64 per cent of the total number of rifles and other weapons, and I apologise, there is something that I forgot. There was also the theft of a cannon. I did not see that at first. My eyesight is not that good. And this raised alarm among people in Bratunac and Srebrenica. First of all, we didn't understand how come a company could have a cannon. Perhaps this is what you're asking me what were legal and what were illegal forms of arming, because the Territorial Defence also distributed some of the arms across the companies in the area and they also gave some trustworthy people some weapons and so on and so forth. However, Feros is a company that was given the cannon from the Territorial Defence to look after it, and during the night that anti-aircraft cannon was stolen which raised concern among the Serb population. The first question was why did they need a cannon, and then when it was stolen, nobody knew how it would be used. That's why we were all afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we please now look at the last page of this document. What happened in late August and early September 1991, which is being referred to in the last paragraph which says after the incident the Muslims gathered on the 4th September? What happened then?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: That was preceded by the killing of two Muslims in Kravica and, even before that, two Serbs were wounded in Avdagina Njiva at a check-point between Kravica and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak slowly and repeat the names of all the toponyms that he is enumerating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think you are speaking too fast so that it's impossible for the interpreters to catch up with your speed, in particular when you are referring to names, et cetera. Could you please slow down and put a pause, wait a moment before you start answering the question. Could you repeat the answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This relates to the period when, between the villages of Glogova and Kravica, two Serbs from Han Pijesak were wounded, seriously wounded from firearms, and this was followed by the killing of two Muslims in the village of Kravica, more precisely in Kajici village, and after that, the vice-president of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Nikola Koljevic, and Avdo Hebiba came with him. He was a high-ranking official of the BH MUP. They came to address the crowd of inhabitants who gathered there. People were afraid. There were two groups. One were the Muslims. The other group were Serbs, and in front of the police station a lot of Muslims got together. Mevludin Sinanovic, if I can see it clearly, climbed on a chair, took a knife out and threatened the Serbs by saying that our country was Serbia and that was the only place where we could live. So that would be more or less what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This report, regardless of the fact that it was drafted by the Muslim-run centre, does it approximately reflect the situation and tensions and incidents in Bratunac municipality?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, President. I said this is very close to the truth with the exception of certain minor details that I might object to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we admitted this, but what Ms. Edgerton wanted to know is within what context witness did see this document. If you'd take a look at his document -- statement, 54, "I have seen -- I have been shown document, this one, Official Note," and he also said, "which I also received." So in what context did he receive this document? Did you receive this Official Note at the time, Mr. Djukanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I received this Official Note at the time when I was the president of the Executive Committee in Bratunac. We were informed about this, and I even have a copy of this paper in my briefcase which I left in my hotel room. I didn't bring it with me. Having talked with the people who testified before me, I was told that I can see the statement on the screen and that questions would be asked of me in that way, so I didn't bring the paper with me. As I said, I have it in my possession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So what you are saying is that that's the usual practice for SDB people to send his -- their report to the -- which is strictly confidential, to the members of the Executive Committee. Is that what you're saying, Mr. Djukanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not claiming that, but this particular document reached my desk. I don't know what classified information is and how the secret services act, but in this particular instance, we had this information. Possibly the reason was to make us aware of the threats aimed at me, Mr. Djukanovic, and everybody else listed here, and later on it turned out that they were valid threats. I was shot at, some people were killed, and some people had to flee the area. All I remember is that I found it on my desk, but I don't know how it came to be in my hands, whether through the protocol or maybe somebody just brought it into my office in order to inform me. Anyway, I still have the document to this date. And I clearly remember that these intelligence officers were registered under specific numbers, which I found odd, but nevertheless, even if the information is confidential, it sometimes find its way into the public domain, the books, diaries, anything you can think of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That concludes your examination-in-chief, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellency. Yes, Your Excellency. That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That concludes your evidence in chief in this case, Mr. Djukanovic. Now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Djukanovic, good morning. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning. I can hear you well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Would you like to have your statement in front of you, with you now, Mr. Djukanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it could be useful, but if I get the documents in good time in Serbian, if I move closer to the screen, then I can follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I just want to start off, Mr. Djukanovic, by -- with a small clarification on one of the paragraphs you added to your witness statement after you saw Dr. Karadzic, and that's paragraph 63 where you make reference to the location of Cerovac, Cerovac. Now, it's correct, isn't it, first of all, that the proper spelling of that location in Bratunac municipality is C-e-r-o-v-a-c? It was misspelled in the adjudicated fact you were shown; correct? The name was simply misspelled.

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you asking me? In my statement, it is correctly spelt Cerovac, exactly as you did it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I was asking you. And just one further clarification. These locations, Cerovac and Polje, are part of the area of Hranca, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They're very close. They may belong to Hranca. These are two hamlets that are probably part of Hranca. But, listen, this place called Polje, actually, I had never heard of it. Cerovac is part of Hranca, but it is possible that it is next to the road, Polje. Sometimes valleys are referred to as Polje in our language, but I have never heard of that place. There is a place called Zapolje, but I don't know about Polje. And what I stated here is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, when you describe Cerovac as being a Serbian village, you don't mean to say that there are no Muslims who live there, do you?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: That's not what I said. There was a Serbian Cerovac and a Muslim Cerovac, and it is possibly that a civil war broke out there. I really don't know when that occurred, and I don't have that information. You have to admit that it's been more than 20 years since then, but I know for sure that the Serbian village Cerovac was completely destroyed by fire and that we accepted people from Cerovac in Bratunac. I clearly remember that. As for the Muslim village of Cerovac, and if I look at this date, I really cannot tell you anything more. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's fine. Now, just a couple of other clarification questions. Your nickname is Rocko, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in your statement that you gave to Dr. Karadzic's Defence, you mentioned -- you talked about the High Representative's decision in 2004. Now, at the time he issued that decision, you were a member of the SDS Main Board; correct?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you were a member of the RS National Assembly; correct?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And how long had you been serving as a member of the SDS Main Board?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the SDS Main Board -- let me think. The replacements took place in 2004, but I think that I served the whole term of office, I believe. I think that the party elections were in 2002. I don't remember exactly. But all I know is that I was a member for quite a long time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How long is quite a long time? When were you first appointed to a position in the SDS Main Board?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I was elected at the Assembly of the Serbian Democratic Party I believe in 2002. Paddy Ashdown dismissed us in 2004.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So two years at least.

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: At least.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. And so those things aren't in your statement, are they?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't mention that. I did say, though, that I was sanctioned by the High Representative, allegedly because I was part of the support network of President Karadzic. Now, after these sanctions were removed and eight years later, it turned out to be untrue. Now as far as this is concerned and as far as these allegations are concerned, they proved to be false and I did not participate in any actions relating to the hiding of President Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I -- I never heard or seen President Karadzic since 1996, and I didn't know his whereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, since you've -- you felt a need to expand on that, let's have a look at the copy of the High Representative's decision at 65 ter number 24810. You don't by any chance read English, do you, Mr. Djukanovic? All right. Then I'll --

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- read to you --

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not literate in English. [In English] From his positions as member of --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated][Overlapping speakers] ... I'll read to you the parts I --

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This is the actual High Representative's decision removing from your positions on the Main Board and the RS Assembly, and if we could go over to page 3 of this document, at the very bottom of that page, the very last paragraph, it says: As a leading member of the SDS occupying a position of responsibility within the party and based on solid information and belief, Rodoljub Djukanovic is, in whole or in part, culpable for the SDS's failure to purge the political landscape of conditions conducive to the sustenance of individuals indicted under Article 19 of the ICTY statute. Mr. Djukanovic's failings are inimical to stability and the rule of law, and Mr. Djukanovic, therefore, obstructs the process of peace, implementation and must be removed from office forthwith. Now, Mr. Djukanovic, I don't see anything in there about harbouring Dr. Karadzic. You were considered to be violating your country's commitments to the peace agreement. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: In this portion that you read it seems to be the case, but you left out of a lot of it. You took it out of the context, because before that, when there is reference to President Karadzic and other indictees accused of war crimes, it seems according to this that we were not exactly co-operative. You understand what I mean, that the -- we were not loyal citizens of our country, that we were not co-operating with The Hague Tribunal, but none of that was true. Nobody asked us to do anything about that. It never happened that somebody called me and I refused to appear. It's all untrue. Therefore, I was not hindering the implementation of the peace process, and I can confirm categorically and by assuming all kinds of responsibilities, criminal and otherwise, that we complied.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: We were --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: -- accused of the indictees of being somewhere and that we were helping them stay where they are. I don't know where he got this information from.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And this was repealed in 2011, following the apprehension of General Mladic; correct? That's -- yes or no. Do you know or don't you?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, after that, but quite some time after that, and I don't see the connection with the apprehension of Mladic. I don't know what -- what the relation could be between these events, and I never thought about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, just a little bit more about your function within the SDS. You only added later on to paragraph 27 of your statement that you were a member of the SDS Municipal Board in Bratunac. Now, just to put some dates in place, can you confirm that that was the case actually from way back in August 1990 right through to 1995?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was a member of the Municipal Board throughout that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you also talked in your statement about your function as head of the Executive Board, but I wonder --

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- if you can confirm that, in fact, following your move to the government of RS in March 1993, you actually, the year after, in August 1994, returned to take up the position of Executive Council president in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I never returned to resume this position. After president came to Bratunac to allow the UNPROFOR convoy to pass through Srebrenica, I and other people on the Executive Committee, at the request of the people who were putting together the Government of Republika Srpska, we decided to nominate the best people and the best educated people, and one of those people who was invited to participate was myself. In 1993 when President Karadzic visited Bratunac, my impression really was that this was becoming a core of something that could be a political guarantee of our property and our safety and security. I believe that this would yield good results, and I decided to join them in order to help with my experience and knowledge in creating institutions. I was appointed the main inspector or the assistant minister. I was not a member of the cabinet, but I was given a large department. When I came, there was nobody at the head of that department, but in 1995, after St. Archangel's day, I refused -- I returned home. I did not resign. I only asked to be allowed to rejoin my family.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Djukanovic, I asked you about 1994, and we actually went from 1993 right through to 1995, so maybe I can help us stay focused by showing you a document. It's -- it's a page from the minutes of the Assembly sessions from the Bratunac SDS, and it has 65 ter number 00603.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, is this document that's leaving our screen going to be tendered by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I want in this document to go to page 55 of the English and B/C/S page 46.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This is -- I'll wait until we see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And page -- I don't see a match. Thank you. If we could just go over there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, these are minutes from a meeting of the Bratunac SDS Municipal Board from 14 August 1994. Now, first of all, we see in the middle of the page on the English and at the bottom of the page in your language that you were present at that meeting. Your name's at the very bottom of page 46 in your language.

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if we can just go over to page 47 in your language and flip over to page 56 in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And in B/C/S it's on the right-hand side of the page under item 4. Page 47 in B/C/S, and page 56 in English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the previous English page was correct, but we lost it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, I have the previous English page. Thank you, Dr. Karadzic. I'm trying to make sure that we have the proper B/C/S page, which should be page 47. And I appreciate it's not easy because of the way these B/C/S pages have been entered into evidence. That helps. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Under item 4 on these pages, we see a decision to unfreeze your status and for you to enter the Municipal Board of Bratunac for the purpose of taking over as the Executive Committee president, which is not what you've just explained to us. So --

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- did you return to become Executive Council president or not?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I was never re-appointed as president of the Executive Committee. Executive Committee is an executive branch, whereas the Municipal Board is something which is called political authority. The period when I joined the Government of Republika Srpska, for a time I did not attend the meetings or anything, and meetings were anyway scarce because of the lack of communications.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear Mr. Karadzic's intervention.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, this means that I was reactivated as a member of the Municipal Board, and I was literally obliged to attend the board meetings, and I was virtually warned of being obliged to come and attend the meetings, but I never resumed the position of the president of the Executive Committee in the executive branch of the government in Bratunac. I cannot remember all the details of this, but I remember what was happening, and there was a lot of criticism coming from Serbia on the account of our leadership.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what happened later.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you. Now that you've cleared that up, I want to go to some of your other SDS positions. Is it correct or can you confirm that later in 1994 you were appointed to the position of director of the distribution centre? October 1994.

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Distribution centre? Distribution of what? Oh, yes, the distribution centre in Bratunac. Yes. Perhaps, though it may have been called slightly differently. What you refer to as the centre for distribution is the distribution centre housed in a facility that was put up by the Swedish, with all of the equipment and ramps belonging to the Guber company. I took it over perhaps in October or November 1995, when I told you I returned from the RS government. Then I became director of Guber, and it also had a distribution centre under it in Bratunac. The distribution per se is just a building which for the most part was empty --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay, thank you --

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: -- and it had -- what do you call them?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's go back now to 1992. And apologies to jump you around like this, but perhaps you can confirm that in June 1992, in addition to your positions in the Municipal Board and on the Crisis Staff, you were also appointed to the War Presidency for Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. Per function, per position, because that was something to be occupied by the president of the Executive Council, and as you can see, I was elected to that post legally and legitimately by all the citizens of Bratunac municipality. There were three political parties, the SDA, SDS, and SDP, and out of 61 deputies, there were only 4 deputies against my appointment. When this happened, what happened in 1992, then I, by virtue of my position as president of Executive Council, became a member of the Crisis Staff for a while during the period when the authorities basically did not even function.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can you also confirm that in addition to these positions you served as a member of the SDS regional board for Birac?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I was elected to the Executive Council of the region of Birac called the SAO Birac at the time. It was a political response of ours to the referendum which took place around that time, because the Muslims and Croats decided to hold a referendum to secede from Yugoslavia. I did not dispute their right as a people to do that, but we as a people refused to accept it. By virtue of the constitution from 1974 it was the right of the peoples, not of the republics. However, they --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Djukanovic, I didn't ask you about what kind of response you had to the referendums. I simply asked you to confirm whether or not you severed as a member of the SDS regional board for Birac. So maybe I could invite you to just focus on what I'm asking you for questions.

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can you also confirm that the members -- among the other members of the SDS Regional Board were Mr. Deronjic, Rajko Dukic, Brano Grujic, and Jovo Mijatovic, among others? Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I can confirm that they were present, and I was there, and I was elected vice-president of the Executive Council of the SAO Birac. Apologies. I just wanted to clarify by saying that it was our political response. It was a political item we rallied around, and we were against the referendum. We wanted to hold a referendum which would be voting on our remaining in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Now, I want to jump forward to 1995 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, Your Honours. You might tell by my voice I'm a bit under the weather today.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So I'd like to move forward to 1995. You said in your statement that in 1995, and I'll find you the exact paragraph reference, in paragraph 53, you were not in Bratunac, and that was in reference to events in Srebrenica in 1995. So I'd just like you to tell us where specifically, physically, you were in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: In July 1995, I was still with the RS government on the jobs I have described, but indeed in July 1995, I was in Bratunac. My cousin had been killed, that is to say, my uncle's brother. I was dressed in black and in mourning. I was in Bratunac for a couple of days and did not follow events --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: -- but in principle, I wasn't in Bratunac during that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When was that? When were you in Bratunac in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I was in Bratunac on the very day when Ibran Mustafic, I don't know the date, but it was when he -- he wrote that book. He was the president of the Executive Council in Srebrenica. If you know when he was brought in to the police station, I don't know if he spent a few days there, but it was on the day I was there. I saw him come out in front of the police station to have a cigarette.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I saw him in front of the station in Bratunac and I do not recall which day it was exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, while you were in Bratunac, did you have -- did the Municipal Assembly meet?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I was not a deputy in the Municipal Assembly of Bratunac. I told you, I was only a member of the Municipal Board, and I do not recall an Assembly session in Bratunac. That's one thing. Another thing, I told you why I came and what my state of mind was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Maybe --

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't care much about things at the time --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Maybe --

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: -- and I didn't follow politics.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Maybe I can show you another document to refresh your memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we go back, please, to 65 ter number 00603.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: These are the minutes of the meetings of the Bratunac Municipal Assembly that I showed you earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's go over in English to page 66, and in B/C/S it should be page 55. And I appreciate my friend's difficulty with the Serbian pages, because in fact two pages of a book have been scanned to make a single page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, here's minutes from the second meeting of the SDS Municipal Board in Bratunac held on July 30th, 1995, and if we scroll -- if we have a look halfway through the page in front of you, we see that you were there, and you see that in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if we could go over in English to page 56. Pardon me. If we could go over in B/C/S to page 56. On the bottom left-hand side and over in English to page 67, I think. Under item -- under item 3 we see there that the Assembly was informed on the situation in the area since the liberation of Srebrenica until that day, July 30th.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And at this meeting, Mr. Djukanovic, you were included on -- in a working group on a platform for the territorial and political integration of the municipalities of Skelani, Srebrenica, and Bratunac along with Mr. Deronjic, Mr. Simic, and Jovan Nikolic. Now is your memory refreshed as to what you were doing on the 30th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I do not dispute that I was there on the 30th of July. I did not know what this pertained to. I think I said something different as regards 1995 and the events in Srebrenica. I wasn't there then, because by the time I was the principal market inspector and I thought you were asking me about something else. On the 30th of July, in Bratunac, at the Assembly, I was there positively because I see my name appear several times. Wherever it says "Rocko," "Rocko's suggestion," that's all true, I was there. And I see Rodoljub Djukanovic appearing as well. Yes. Yes. I attended this session of the Assembly. Is there anything in dispute there?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, I'm happy to have your confirmation because it was clarification of your statement to the effect that you weren't in Bratunac around the time of the events in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to tender the pages related to this meeting as an exhibit, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you tendering the previous pages we saw, pages -- English pages 55 and 56?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I -- I think it's -- yes, because that covers the whole meeting that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When Mr. Stevic was here we admitted part of this document, so in that regard we'll admit separately the document parts we saw today as separate exhibit. Shall we give the number.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I did note that other pages had been previously tendered and I'm in Your Honours' hands as to how to organise that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the dates we are admitting is 14th of August and -- 1994 and 30th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6237, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in your evidence you discussed -- actually, I'll ask you the question a different way. These SDS meetings that we've been looking at, the meetings that you attended, discussed, Mr. Djukanovic, orders and directives you received from Dr. Karadzic and from the SDS central authorities, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Listen, these were no orders by Dr. Karadzic to establish a region or a town that would include Srebrenica and Bratunac. I know there were such proposals by some people who perhaps were not well versed. You know how it is. There are people -- there are tradesmen who wish to be architects, et cetera. These were different matters. But from Karadzic we never received anything in that regard. I know that Miroslav Deronjic was appointed some kind of a civilian commissioner for Srebrenica. That's what I know. Now --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Djukanovic --

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: -- as for any direct instructions --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When you say that -- when you say that, do you mean to say that you never received orders from Dr. Karadzic at any time during the war? Or even prior?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, in what capacity? In what capacity could he have received it, or received it as what, as the president of the Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. It's not appropriate for you to intervene in such a way. You can take up the issue. Ms. Edgerton can ask the witness whether he received any order, instruction, or whatever. Please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Would you like me to repeat my question, Mr. Djukanovic?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: No need. I understood the question well. Trust me, irrespective of President Karadzic's intervention, I never, be it in oral or written form, received from President Karadzic any kind of order to do something which would indicate anything improper. I don't know what you mean exactly, really, but I didn't --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: -- at least --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't ask about whether or not it was something proper or improper. I asked whether at any time in the period up to or during the conflict in former Yugoslavia you received orders or directives from Dr. Karadzic. And actually, just to make it perfectly clear, I'm not talking about you personally. I'm talking about you within your function - and I hope this assists Dr. Karadzic - within your function in the municipal and SDS authorities in Bratunac, did you receive any orders or directives from Dr. Karadzic; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's all I wanted, Your Excellency. To see to what position my instructions should have or were supposed to go to.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness started speaking and overlapping. Could he please start again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, when I said inappropriate, just be patient. You can clarify during your re-examination. Because of your intervention, witness was not heard. Could you repeat your answer, Mr. Djukanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I told you I have never, in written or oral form, officially or unofficially, and that's what I usually say, I never received any orders from Mr. Karadzic, any orders to do something, because I was part of the executive authority. I was the principal market inspector and only a member of the Municipal Board, and the president of the Municipal Board was Miroslav Deronjic. Politically speaking -- sorry, I'll try to slow down. He was tasked with communicating with President Karadzic when there were Main Board meetings at the party, et cetera. Now, there was a period during which the work of our political party was frozen, that is to say of the SDS. I don't recall when exactly --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: First and foremost so that there would be no party politics undertaken by just about anyone --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: -- that's why we froze the work of the party.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How about -- how about we have a look again at another document because I think that will help focus you really.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This time I'd like to have a look at P3197. Now, this is another set of minutes, P3197. This is another set of minutes and it's minutes of the emergency meeting of the Municipal Board of the SDS of Bratunac. Page -- in B/C/S pages 2 to 4. Not the correct B/C/S page. Start by going to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll -- what I'll do is I'll read this to you, and if we need to go back to this after the break or if you'd like to see the original copy --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you know -- Madam Registrar [sic], if you could go back one page in B/C/S. And it's because of the way these have been scanned. And again one page, please. There we are.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, these are minutes of a meeting which you see in the second paragraph which is at the bottom of the page in your language, which you see specifically relate to a meeting of -- an enlarged session of the Main Board of the SDS in BiH. Mr. Deronjic informed all those present about the positions and instructions of the Main Board of the SDH [sic] after an enlarged session was held last night October 18, 1991, and Mr. -- Mr. Djukanovic, underneath the heading of this document you see specifically that these are minutes of an emergency meeting related to the order of the president of the SDS BiH, Dr. Karadzic. How could that be any clearer? And -- and, Mr. Djukanovic, this Court has received evidence that shows that Dr. Karadzic, on the 18th of October, declared a state of emergency in the party, and the SDS across Bosnia and Herzegovina was instructed to take specific measures. Here we have a clear example of the SDS in Bratunac meeting to take specific measures in response to an order from Dr. Karadzic following an enlarged session of the SDS Main Board. So this appears again to directly contradict what you said in your evidence a few minutes ago, does it not?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I didn't completely or entirely understand you. I don't know what it's about. I told you that in terms of communicating with President Karadzic, it was -- well, perhaps it wasn't necessarily his task, but it was part of his job description who was the president of the Municipal Board, and it was Miroslav Deronjic, who was also a member of the Main Board. Now, as for an order arriving from Radovan Karadzic, I don't know what you wanted to say. Was it an order to establish a Crisis Staff or to declare some kind of extraordinary measures or state? Ex officio as the president of the board I was a member of the staff. It's nothing to be disputed. Everyone knows that in times of crisis such staffs are formed, let alone in the type of chaos we lived in.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You said unequivocally, actually, that you never received orders or directives from Dr. Karadzic, and that was in answer to my question. And these minutes of this Assembly meeting, which appears to be on the 19th of October, 1991, say exactly the contrary. So which is correct, Mr. Djukanovic?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: You're trying to say that at the Assembly session an order arrived from President Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Djukanovic, you said you never received orders from Dr. Karadzic. These Assembly minutes say exactly the opposite. Look at the title line: "Minutes of the emergency meeting of the Presidency of the Municipal Board of the SDS of Bratunac related to the order of the president of the SDS of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Dr. Karadzic." What's unclear about that? Mr. Djukanovic, you did receive orders from Dr. Karadzic, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well -- well, I said I didn't receive any orders from Dr. Karadzic for a long time, and Miroslav liked to use his political skill and would tell us that it was ordered by Dr. Karadzic, whereas, as a matter of fact, he actually wanted to put forth something of his own, perhaps to deal with a political opponent. It was this or that. But I don't see any kind of orders sent by President Karadzic. You can only see that these are the minutes of the emergency meeting of the Presidency of the Municipal Board of the SDS of Bratunac related to the order of the president of the SDS of BH, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So is it your evidence that you --

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see it ever or -- I'm listening.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I interrupted you. You can finish your sentence.

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I'm listening. You asked me if I was saying --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So are you saying that you in Bratunac then took no special measures as a result of this order from Dr. Karadzic and the positions and instructions of the Main Board of the SDS declaring a state of emergency?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I told you that Miroslav Deronjic would bring these sort of opinions, and we of course trusted him. But to tell you the truth, he frequently used his political skill to forward his own agenda.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So are you saying --

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't see any orders by Dr. Karadzic in here.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So these minutes don't reflect anything from Dr. Karadzic. This reflects Mr. Deronjic's own agenda. Is that what you're saying now?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Most likely, because I don't see any kind of paper. Is there proof that there was an order? It says on orders from Dr. Karadzic, but I don't see any orders. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How about --

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: To establish Crisis Staffs? What did this pertain to, and what was supposed to be done? Briefing on the situation after an illegal vote of the -- about the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We did discuss such matters, and it's not disputed. And that there may have been such an order by Dr. Karadzic, but I didn't have it in my hand. I probably must have accepted it, and I don't recall it all too well. I don't recall the meeting either. I see I was in attendance because it's in the minutes, but to tell you the truth, I don't know what it is. Is there a mistake in there? I said -- actually, I swore to tell the truth and nothing but the truth, and what I'm saying is 100 per cent truth. If I don't remember it, you have to accept it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you don't remember -- you don't remember that you were --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if we could go over to -- slide over to the next page in B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 20 in the transcript, the witness said: "Even if there had been such a thing, there's nothing in dispute. Even if Karadzic's order had existed, I don't see anything in dispute there." And he said also: "You have to accept that I may have forgotten things, that there are things that I don't remember." That's on page 35. I'm again asking the witness to speak slowly. I am sure that the interpreters are having a very hard time in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Shall we take a break if it is convenient?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, of course. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When we return, I would like you to speak very slow, Mr. Djukanovic. We'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Djukanovic, before we broke, Dr. Karadzic noted that on the transcript you effectively disputed any order from Dr. Karadzic having issued on the 18th of October. You said, "I don't see any kind of paper. Is there proof that there was an order?" So I'd like to show you some proof, all right?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have a look at 65 ter number 03322. It's a telegram from Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you check the number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, I think you meant P332.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sure I must have. Thank you, Mr. Robinson. No. Let me -- indulge me for a moment and I'll speak with Mr. Reid. And in the meanwhile I can go to another document, 65 ter number 00964, and I hope I've got that number right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This is, Mr. Djukanovic, a telegram from Dr. Karadzic to the Municipal Board of the SDS in Zavidovici, and it says: "... I," pursuant to statutory authorisations, "hereby announce the SDS state of emergency mandatory for all its organs, members, and personnel in the authorities. You will receive daily instructions on measures regarding the state of emergency ..." And it's dated 18 October 1991, the same date as the orders, the minutes of the emergency meeting of the Bratunac Municipal Board of the SDS that we have been talking about. Do you maintain that the Bratunac SDS received no orders from Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: May I? May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I stated that I had never seen this. I never received any orders from Dr. Radovan Karadzic. Now that you have shown this to me, I considered a telegram did arrive at the municipal -- Municipal Board in Zavidovici, if this is indeed authentic, and I don't doubt it. I'm not disputing that that happened, but I did not see it, and I am testifying on my own behalf. It was a matter of debate at the meeting of the Municipal Board, and I could also see that from the document that you showed me, everything that we saw in the minutes where it says that we decided on a plebiscite. Actually, it was a referendum of the Serbian people, and I believe that before that I had said that we decided to stay in Yugoslavia, and that was the topic of our discussion at the meeting of the Municipal Board. I do not dispute that. I do not dispute the fact that you asked me nothing about, but I suppose you will, that I became a member of the Crisis Staff that was set up -- or, rather, there was a proposal to establish the Crisis Staff. You will probably have a document to show me when it became operational. I am not denying the fact that as the president of the Municipal Board, by virtue of that position I automatically became a member of the Crisis Staff. I don't see anything in dispute there. I don't see us contradicting each other in any way. You asked --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Djukanovic --

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: -- me whether we received or not -- yes, I'm with you. I'm listening.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My question was whether you maintained that the SDS board in Bratunac received no orders from Dr. Karadzic, having seen this document and having looked at the minutes relating to the order of 18 October 1991. And your answer was about personally receiving orders. My question is about the SDS board for Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. Well, listen, let me tell you, when I said that I never received anything from President Karadzic I was speaking on my own behalf. When it comes to the Municipal Board, it was Miroslav Deronjic who conveyed messages to us, and I told you that after such a long time I could not remember the course of the meeting itself. I can't tell you that I remember what Miroslav told us. However, based on the document that you have just shown me, I can see that Miroslav was the one who put us abreast of the situation, that we accept his report, and that based on that we selected organs for the referendum. Like, for example, you -- Jovan Nikolic and then members of the executive staff -- or, rather, the Crisis Staff, I don't know what you want to call it. Some members were chosen, and I was among those people. This is correct. So I don't know. I don't see that there is any contradiction there between the two of us. I don't see us being at diametrically opposite positions. I'm only telling you that I did not see Dr. Karadzic's order. It arrived in Zavidovici, and if it arrived in Bratunac, it must have reached the hands of the president of the board. There's nothing in dispute there. We did opt for a referendum in order to stay in Yugoslavia and that was contrary to the attempts of the other two peoples who wanted to secede from Yugoslavia. They as peoples wanted to separate Bosnia and Herzegovina from the rest of the state.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I have this document, please, as a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6238, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So along this line, when you at paragraph 27 of your statement said you were not aware that the party leadership, politicians, or President Karadzic himself sent any plans to municipalities referring to some Variants A and B, were you speaking in terms of your own personal knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was an important member of the SDS. After all, I was a member of the Municipal Board. I was the President of the Executive Board. I was a member of the political and executive authorities there, so I should have been aware of that. I'm telling the whole truth, and in my statement I stated that I had never heard of any plans A, B, although I believe that Miroslav would have informed me about the existence of such a plan if there was indeed such a plan. That's why I'm surprised by the fact that I did not receive the paper that you are showing me for municipality of Zavidovici. I'm sure that I would have been given that paper if there had been some plans in place as you are putting to me. I should have been abreast. I should have known, but I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's go back to 65 ter number 00603, minutes of the meetings of the Municipal Assembly of Bratunac municipality, English translation page 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me. These minutes are actually identified as the minutes of the Assembly of the SDS party, not the Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Apologies. And I accept your correction. English page 12. And rather than count the B/C/S page, I'll give you the ERN number that appears at the top of the page. It's 02192721.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, these, Mr. Djukanovic, are minutes of a meeting of the Bratunac SDS Municipal Board, dated 23 December 1991, and it's a meeting to consider the material from the SDS Presidency in Sarajevo. A decision was reached to form the Serbian BiH, Bosnia and Herzegovina. This -- it refers to two variants, A and B, which were proposed. For Bratunac, the Variant B was envisaged. Second level of organisation. Now, Mr. Djukanovic, as an important member, as you've just described yourself, of the SDS in Bratunac, who would have seen, as you've just said, this document, and being confronted now with the minutes where the document was discussed, how can you maintain that you never heard about the Variant A and B document?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you're trying to say that I am not telling the truth, but I did tell the truth, and I swore that I would tell the truth. I really wasn't aware of any plans A or B. I am looking at the minutes. I don't know whether I attended that meeting. But I can see that there is reference to some duty, detail, a Crisis Staff. I did tell you that I'd been elected to a Crisis Staff. That's a fact. In my view, that was upon the insistence of Mr. Miroslav Deronjic. Please do not make me refer to dead people. I don't want to say anything bad about that person, but as I've told you, Miroslav sometimes --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to refer to dead people. I'm asking you -- I'm asking you how in your capacity, if you were as in the know as you claim to be, you, confronted with these minutes, now maintain you never heard of the Variant A and B document?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Impossible to translate.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you repeat your comment, please.

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Miroslav Deronjic was one of the vice-presidents. There's nothing to repeat. Miroslav Deronjic was a member of the SDS Presidency in Sarajevo, and this seems to be discussing materials from the SDS Presidency in Sarajevo. And as it says here, he said something that I cannot read. He presented the material and then they moved on to item 1. A decision was made on the establishment of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Two variants are envisaged, A and B. For us Variant B was envisaged and in terms of the level of organisation. Believe me, I don't remember this. I don't know what these Variants A and B are. What does this refer to? I cannot establish any links. I said in my statement that I was not aware of the existence of any variants and especially not of the fact that we were supposed to fall under Variant B. I really don't have a clue. And as for Zavidovici, Zavidovici is a very specific municipality which is in the federation, in the Central Bosnia-Herzegovina. There may have been a state of emergency there. I don't have a clue. I don't know what the situation was like there at the moment because the chaos already started reigning supreme in the state. And I really don't know that there were any Variants A and B for Bratunac. I don't know what Variant A was as opposed to Variant B. Please can you show me whether I attended this session of the Municipal Council. Is that the same session and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the date. Could the witness please be instructed to slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you tell me whether I attended this meeting? Did I make an intervention that would --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Djukanovic -- Mr. Djukanovic --

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: -- that would demonstrate that I --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The interpreters continue to have a difficult time following you because you speak so quickly. Could you please make an effort, for their sake and the clarity of the record, to slow down. And I would invite you to focus on the questions, because you seem to have a tendency to answer things that are not posed to you. Now, you said that if this had been concerning some official party document, you would have known about it, and you said that in your statement. So --

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Because you've not heard of this document you think it's not an official party document even though the Crisis Staff that you became a member was determined to be constituted at this 23 December meeting pursuant to these instructions? So you became a member of the Crisis Staff. The Crisis Staff was formed, and you became a member on the basis of an unofficial document?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether I was already a member. It stems from this that this was just a proposal. I'm surprised by the fact that I'm at the last place in that Crisis Staff. I believe that I occupied a place that would have been closer to the top. I can see that everybody is above me. I am at the bottom of that list. I don't even know whether I attended that meeting but I claim that I am not aware of any A or B variants. This is your key question. This is a key issue here; right? And I have already answered that I am not aware of Variant A or B. This is what you asked me. And as for me being a member of the Crisis Staff, I was a member. There was a proposal on the table. It was meant to be -- become operational in a state of emergency.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's go -- let's leave this document and go to another meeting, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you tender this page, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: -- it's already in evidence as Exhibit P2598.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You know, Mr. Djukanovic, this document, this Variant A and B document, was recovered in locations like Livno, and that's P3470; the Boksit office at the Holiday Inn, and that's P960; a briefcase found in Dr. Karadzic's apartment, P005. This Chamber has received evidence from Defence witnesses that this document was distributed to Mr. Grujic, the SDS president in Zvornik, and that's T 17227. It's received evidence from witnesses that it was implemented by the SDS party in locations like Ilidza, in Sarajevo; that's T 35210 and T 12952. And Dr. Karadzic himself in 1995, at the 50th Assembly session, and you said you were an assemblyman - and that's P970, pages 316 in English and 970 in B/C/S - specifically referred to this document. He said: "You will remember the A and B Variants. In the B variant, where we were in the minority, 20 per cent, 15 per cent, we had set up a government and a brigade, a unit, no matter what size, but there was a detachment with a commander," and then further he says, "distribution of weapons was carried out thanks to the JNA." So for a man as integrated in the SDS and municipality structures as you were, as influential as you claim to be, Mr. Djukanovic, it rings hollow your assertion that you had never heard of the Variant A and B document, particularly so when it's discussed during a meeting of the Bratunac SDS Municipal Board short days after it was distributed in Sarajevo. So, Mr. Djukanovic, did you hear about it or didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I've already told you that I did not hear of the Variants A and B. I don't know what was going on in Livno. I'm testifying on my own behalf. I don't know what you found in Livno and Zvornik, what kind of documents. I would like you to show me --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So your answer is no. Your answer is no.

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: My answer is that I did not know of the A and B Variant plan. That's my answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay. We'll move on. Now, you spoke in your statement about the armed soldiers --

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- who arrived in Bratunac in April 1992, and they moved into the Hotel Fontana, and that was in paragraph 29. And in paragraph 31 you said: "To this day, I do not know who brought that unit to Bratunac." So as I understand your evidence then, this is -- by that point in time in April, this is after the division of the police; correct?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. The police was split later. You're saying that a group of soldiers, some 20 of them, were billeted in Fontana Hotel after the split in the police. As far as I know, the split in the police came later. So it seems to me that the link that you're establishing is wrong. The police was divided later.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How about I ask you the question another way. So your evidence, integrated into the municipal government structures as you were, is that you don't know who brought these paramilitaries in. Mr. Djukanovic, it was you who brought them in, wasn't it? It was the SDS board from Bratunac who was most active in the preparations for the organisation of the Serbian people in Bratunac. And it was you, together with Mr. Deronjic, who facilitated their arrival into the town. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Not correct. I apologise for telling you that you're not telling the truth. It is simply not correct. It's simply not true. Those people came from somewhere, and they just turned up in front of Fontana Hotel one morning. None of us had known about their arrival, and I claim that with full responsibility.
