Maybe somebody knew, but I as somebody, as a factor in the authorities, in the state, I didn't know about that. I was surprised that not even Mr. Deronjic or Mr. Nikolic or anybody in my vicinity knew about that. None of the members of that so-called Crisis Staff, which was never established -- or, rather, it was just a proposal before the war activities started. Some people arrived. Nobody knew them, and their commander's name was Zan, and I put it very nicely in my statement. That man invited me and Deronjic, Nijaz Dubicic, Mirsad Kavazbasic, the president of the SDA, the president of the Assembly, and the president of Srebrenica municipality, Besim Ibisevic, he invited us to a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now you're repeating your statement, so we'll move on. And you accuse me of not telling the truth, but I'll tell you why I asked the question, because on the 6th of May, 1992, General Mladic, General Mladic, received information from General Mandaric -- and I'll let you have a look where he recorded that information. It's in P1477, and it's General Mladic's notebook on 6 May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could go to the B/C/S typewritten page. That would be page 258, and the English pages are 253 to 255.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, on that date, General Mladic noted -- he was getting a briefing on the situation from General Mandaric. Nikola Mandaric, Mr. Djukanovic, at that time was the JNA 1st Military District Chief of Staff. And Mandaric says on 6th of May, a front has opened up on the Drina. In Bratunac, two representatives of the SDS are killing all Muslims by slitting their throats. Rodoljub Djukanovic, the president of the SDS, and Rodoljub [sic] Deronjic, two detachments from Bratunac TO, they brought in all the cut-throats from Vukovar and killed everyone they laid their hands on in Hranca near Milici. So I asked the question because the JNA Chief of Staff for the 1st Military District was telling General Mladic he had some information to the contrary. It was you who actually facilitated their arrival into Bratunac, wasn't it, Mr. Djukanovic?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Believe me that nothing here that I see, I see this is some working book of General Mladic. Hranca is not in Bratunac. This is all kind of mish-mash. It has nothing to do with the truth, and to tell you frankly, neither I nor Mr. Deronjic facilitated anyone's arrival. The war spilled over into Bosnia from Croatia, and these people came on their own, this whirlwind of war, and I don't think this is true. I'm not sure that this was actually written by General Mladic. I don't know who fed him this information. And General Mandaric never came to Bratunac. And the use of such words such as cut-throat are such ugly, heinous words and I would never use them in my life. Not only I, nobody amongst us was prepared to commit any crime of that nature. I already said nobody issued any instruction telling us to behave in that manner. All these people didn't have proper names. They all came with nicknames like Zan, Rambo, Djumbo [phoen], Makedonac [phoen], Bugarin [phoen]. There were all nationalities among them, including Muslims, and I tend to believe that there were even Croats among them. It was a motley crew. But to tell you the truth, there were no people that we had known before and that we had invited to come over.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I want to go to another area which is probably going to take me about the next ten minutes, and it's because you said, oddly enough, in your statement that in the -- as far as I can remember, between April and July 1992, and that was at paragraph 51, there was practically no communication between Bratunac and Pale, or if it did exist, it was irregular, difficult, and inadequate. But I want to show you, actually, how well informed Dr. Karadzic and the political and military leadership of the RS were about the situation in Bratunac during this period.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could go to P1478. That's another notebook of General Mladic, and I'd like to go to -- first to English pages 93 and B/C/S typewritten page 93 as well, please. This records General Mladic's notes on consultations on 6 June 1992, on the military and political situation in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina with leading representatives of the state and political leadership. So if we flip over to page 94 -- oh, now, I don't need the handwritten pages. Now, we see that Dr. Karadzic is president -- present at this meeting with General Mladic. And if we go over to page 95 in both versions, we see that Mr. Koljevic, Dr. Koljevic -- the next page in the B/C/S, please, as well. Dr. Koljevic was there as well. And if you flip over to page 98 in English and page 97 in the typewritten B/C/S, you see that Velibor Ostojic is present.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And after that, Mr. Djukanovic, you'll see, if I was to show you the whole meeting, a range of political and municipal leaders were present at this meeting. But if we can now go over to page 101 in both languages, there's a briefing there from Bratunac municipality, and it says: "There are no Muslims left in Bratunac municipality. It's a fully liberated town. There are even no villages which cut off the roads." So contrary to what you say, in June 1992, when you say communication is poor, Dr. Karadzic and his political colleagues as well as his military commanders were fully apprised of the situation in Bratunac, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: What I'm looking at here, when it says "from Bratunac municipality" and then it says "Bratunac is a fully liberated town," frankly speaking, I don't know. Even though I would have liked to have been informed about everything that was going on, for example, I wanted to know everything about the trial of Professor Miroslav Deronjic, this resembles a statement that he made about his brief in the political leadership. But you have to bear in mind that Miroslav Deronjic has struck a deal with you, the Prosecution, and that he sometimes went even further from what you asked him to do because he had been ordered to do so in order to save his family. He believed to have been punished --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Djukanovic, how does that --

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: -- too harshly, but I don't know what --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- answer my question? How does that answer my question? My question --

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you're saying --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My question --

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: -- that you are well informed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My question was this: Contrary to what you say was the case in June 1992, Dr. Karadzic and his political and military leadership were fully apprised of the situation in Bratunac. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, look. Maybe you should better ask Dr. Radovan Karadzic about this, because I really don't know whether he was so well informed. This resembles Miroslav Deronjic's statement to the effect that he managed to break through to Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Djukanovic, why do you keep referring to Mr. Deronjic when I never ask you a question about Mr. Deronjic? Not one. I asked you a question about communication because you said that communication was poor. And I'm going to ask you one more question about communication. We're going to keep with this diary for a minute.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's go to page 246 in e-court, English, and page 244 of the B/C/S typewritten version. And that records a lengthy meeting on 30 June 1992, that Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic had in Zvornik, and that included the presidents of Bratunac, Zvornik, Vlasenica, Sekovici, and Srebrenica, along with military commanders. And you see at number 3 of the attendees, Mr. Simic was there. So let's go over to what Mr. Simic says at page 256 in B/C/S and 258 in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Simic --

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to Ljubisa Simic, the president of Bratunac municipality? Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Simic says: "According to the last census, it was 64-36 in favour of the Muslims. In Bratunac municipality, we now have two Muslims." So any -- Mr. -- Mr. Djukanovic, any expression or view on your part that communication was poor and -- with Pale and that it might have been difficult or inadequate is actually completely unsustainable, isn't it, Mr. Djukanovic? The municipal and military leadership here on the 30th of June, precisely when you said there was practically no communication between Bratunac and Pale, are meeting with the Supreme Commander and the Commander-in-Chief and telling him there's only two Muslims left in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say that there was no communication whatsoever. I said that we had difficulties, and it's not in dispute. That's what I stated in my statement. But I cannot say that there were no communications at all. The president came over in 1993 to help UNPROFOR. So he did somehow find a way of communicating with us. As far as I can see, I wasn't present at this meeting, but that is immaterial. If Ljubisa Simic was there, that's the main point. And you said that this meeting took place in Zvornik? Is that what you said? Was that in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Zvornik. All right. I said that communication was difficult and almost nonexistent, but I never said that there was no communication at all. You cannot make me say that, because that is not true.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be all from me, Your Honours. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Mr. Karadzic, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellency. Let's start with the most recent question about communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In paragraph 42, Mr. Djukanovic, you say that during that period there was no communication with Pale. You speak about Glogova in May. What did you mean by saying "in that period"?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that was the period, Mr. President, when there was fiercest fighting in the area of Bratunac. As far as I know, the passage of the JNA, which we considered the only legitimate armed force, was hindered because everybody else was considered by us as illegal and paramilitary formations. There was an agreement between our local president - and I hope that the Prosecutor will not accuse me of referring to Mr. Deronjic again - but the passage of an army was hindered at one point in the village of Hranca that resulted in dead and wounded. And at one time a decision was made to straight the front line in the area of Glogova, which is now a Bosniak village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that. We are now on page 255 at the moment. Does it say here that Captain Izet work for the TO, that Captain Todorovic received a salary, that there was led in Svetozarevo [phoen], et cetera. What was the nationality of Captain Izet?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: He was a Muslim who was fighting on our side, as far as I know. If we are thinking about the same thing. I know that there was an Izet who was fighting alongside Serbs in this area where Captain Todorovic operated, and this is all I know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I kindly ask you to look at what Mr. Simic is saying: "We are standing in the same place for a long time, and we have become lax." Is Mr. Simic actually complaining or boasting that there were two Muslims in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that he was expressing regret over that fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. It calls for a completely speculative answer, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not guesswork. We were all sorry for all the Muslim families that had to leave Bratunac because they feared for their safety, and they did it on their own initiative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I agree with Ms. Edgerton. The Chamber agrees with Ms. Edgerton's observation. Please move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean President Ljubisa Simic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Of course I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you two co-operate?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did, and we had good co-operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you discuss the issue of the departure of both Muslims and Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We discussed these topics and other topics as well, including military logistics, the departure of Muslims from Bratunac, and the topic of providing assistance to anyone regardless of whether they were Serbs or Muslims. And we selflessly provided this aid without expecting any commendations or citations on expressions of gratitude. So that was a proper way to do things. We were sort of authorities in that period. We were not proper authorities, and we did our best to help people as much as we could. I know that Mr. Simic, with regard to Mr. Izet, who is unfortunately deceased, he provided him in a car -- with a car and offered him to take some people with him. Unfortunately, he left on his own, whereas the people gathered outside the municipal building. They were asking for help. They wanted buses to be provided to them. They wanted help for their children. They asked for food, and we did what we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the two of you share the same attitude towards the relocation or the departure of the population, and were you aware of what I thought about that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That question, in my submission, Your Honours, goes outside of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, can we have, then, page 98. Let's see what this document says or what is recorded in this document. 98, 98. It seems that my words are being quoted. Just a moment. Can we scroll down page 98. Possibly this is the beginning of my contribution. We need, actually, the previous page, the bottom of the previous page. Two pages back. One more, please. We have different numbers on the top and the bottom of the pages. Now, this is the correct page. On the top we have 96, and on the bottom we have 97. Can we now have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please read the very end of my contribution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. The -- Ms. Edgerton raised this, discussed this with the witness to hear about the lack of communication he referred to in his statement, not in relation to the subject matter. So could you tell us how it arises from the line of cross-examination of Ms. Edgerton? Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Ms. Edgerton didn't just deal with that topic but the actual substance of what was conveyed to this witness as reflected in General Mladic's notebooks, two Muslims left in Bratunac, things like that. I think this goes directly to show that -- what Dr. Karadzic's position was and how that was also being conveyed to people in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I think in that regard we can allow the question. Please proceed. Ms. Edgerton, would you like to add anything?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In a non-leading way, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djukanovic, did you know what my position was concerning the right of civilians, particularly with regard with their departure and relocation?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was aware of your views from the very time when the party was founded. And it says here quite clearly we must not pressure people to have displaced [as interpreted]. And I think this was faithfully recorded, and we shared this same attitude.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not understand what witness was saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Djukanovic. Mr. Djukanovic. Mr. Djukanovic, could you kindly repeat your answer from the start very slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am aware of the president's position in this respect, and it says here, and I quote: "We must not exert pressure on the people to move." And that was the attitude that both the president and we shared.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's go back to the issue of communications. Did you as the president of the municipal government have any communication, and how often, either with me or anyone else at Pale at the beginning of war, that is to say, prior to the 30th of June, because this Mladic's note is dated the 30th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I said that we had poor communication and that as far as I personally am concerned, I had communicated with you very rarely, and I already said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Today on page 101 of this document it was recorded that somebody said that Bratunac was a fully liberated town. Can you tell the Chamber what was the size of the territory in Bratunac that was under your control on the 30th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: The only territory we had under our control was the territory of the town itself on the 30th of June. And I think that only in the area of Glogova and Hranca where it says that the passage of the JNA was hindered was something that was altered. I think that was under our control as well with the exception of Kravica who had their own control point because of the front line being criss-crossed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It was not recorded that: "We did not have our internal communications working, let alone any communication with you in Pale." Can you please wait, because it was not recorded that you confirmed that this is correct, and let us both speak more slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the witness's answer. Maybe if he would be kind enough to move closer to the mike.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were too quick.

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I said I agree, President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were too quick again.

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: It's a deal, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you confirm that this sentence which I quoted was not recorded in the transcript, that you said, "We did not have any internal communication, let alone communication with you in Pale"? Do you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 48 you were asked about the notes and what General Mandaric told General Mladic on the 6th of May, 1992. Whose generals were those two in that period on the 6th of May?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 6th of May the two were the JNA generals, because at that time the Army of Republika Srpska had not yet been established.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the position and the attitude of the municipal authorities at the time vis-a-vis the paramilitary formations that you said appeared as volunteers initially and then continued to operate as paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Our attitude was that they were undesirable elements in our territory. We even adopted a decision to expel them from our area. However, people assembled, some say spontaneously, somebody said under someone's influence, but whatever the case may be, we were going through a difficult period, and we were at risk, and our own safety was in danger. Some of these units remained in the area, but we respected the JNA as the only legitimate force. According to the information that we had, the JNA was given the dead-line of 17th of May to withdraw from Bosnia-Herzegovina. According to what they said, this deadline was extended up to the 29th of May, and they abided by it. I don't know who set up this deadline.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djukanovic. I don't have too much time either.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have D3116.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So on the 6th of May, Mandaric had a talk with Mladic, probably on the phone, in which he accused you and Deronjic of having brought in these paramilitary formations and that the Serbs are cutting throats.

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I see he did, but what he said was not true. It was not so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next page, please. The one after that. We could see a better page before. I don't know what this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In any case, I'll read it out in English. Although you understand English as well. [In English] "Serbian Republic of BH, SAO Birac, Bratunac municipality, Crisis Staff, Bratunac 6th of May, 1992. "On the basis of the decision of the National Security Council of the Serbian Republic of BH, and pursuant to the SAO Birac Crisis Staff Decision, and Decision of the Commissioner of the Government of the Serbian Republic of BH for the Birac area, the Bratunac Municipality Crisis Staff hereby takes the following decision: "All paramilitary formations should leave the territory of Bratunac municipality by 1600 hours on 7th of May ..." [Interpretation] Perhaps the conditional "should" in the translation is somewhat softer than the original, but in any case, do you recall when issued this decision and whether this is the decision in question?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: This is the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There's a more legible original, and I think the "should" should have been translated as "must."

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, must.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we next have D3117, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So we can see what sort of decisions you made prior to the 6th of May.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the page where the text of the decision is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did Mandaric ever come or spoke on the phone with any one of you in Bratunac, with you, or that you learned of him talking to someone else?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No one from the circle of people making up the Crisis Staff at the time, and I stand by it. I didn't see him there ever either, and I didn't hear of his coming there or talking to anyone. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So on the 1st of May, pursuant to a decision of the National Security Council of the Serbian Republic of BH on declaring an imminent threat of war and pursuant to the Crisis Staff decision and so on and so forth, you issued this order forbidding all paramilitary formations and illegal citizens, probably illegally armed citizens, to act in the area of Bratunac municipality. Do you recall having reached this decision?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I do. I see that it was signed by Zoran Tesic. He was one of the members of the Crisis Staff. He was probably standing in for Miroslav at the time because he may have been away, but I do recall an order of this kind being issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 45 of today's transcript, you were quoted -- or, actually, you were suggested that the Municipal Board of the SDS was at its most active in preparing the Serbian people of Bratunac. Can you tell us what were the competencies of civilian authorities in the domain of defence at the time the JNA still existed in Bosnia and Herzegovina? What could you and dared do?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Believe me, it was a period of time when even some kind of military administration should have been imposed. We as the civilian authorities for them basically did not even exist, and we did not dare meddle in military affairs. It simply wouldn't work. Not only that we didn't dare, but we shouldn't have. The army is the army, and the civilian police stayed away as well. That is my answer to your question. We tried to set up local authorities and some kind of administration to maybe provide logistics and food for the army. That was the thrust of our activity. But as for any important decisions that would have to do with combat activities and operations, well, we didn't take part in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you the head of the executive branch in Bratunac before the war?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Not only the Variants A and B or did you receive any kind of party documents containing instructions or orders as the executive branch? Did you receive anything of the kind from the party?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I've said already, and I'm prepared to be held criminally liable in case this is disproven, I assert that this is the truth. We did -- I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you establish the Crisis Staff pursuant to the decision or was it a telegram of the 23rd of December? Or how did you go about establishing the Crisis Staff and when?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff was formed later on. I'm not saying that there weren't certain proposals as we could see in the minutes, but the Crisis Staff was formed precisely when the crisis began, when the first casualties in Bratunac occurred and people were upset. Serbs were fleeing to Serbia, Muslims were fleeing too, and we were receiving refugees from Zenica. It was a time of crisis where we had to have a working body which would attempt to address the crisis, to alleviate it, or to perhaps reach a better situation in order to establish the functioning of authorities and the rule of law. That's what we were taught. I had worked for 21 years in state administration by that time, so I was a long-standing civil servant, and many of us had previous experience. Ultimately, the Crisis Staff -- I'm sorry to expand, but it was comprised of teachers, high school teachers, such as Miroslav Deronjic. He was -- he even studied in France as an exceptional student. He was sent to teach there. He could speak languages. There was Ljubisav Simic. Then Tesic, who was a civil engineer. Momir Nikolic, who was indicted and sentenced before this court, he had a national defence degree in -- from Sarajevo. There was also Zoran Radic. So we all did what we knew how to do and we also had someone familiar with the laws of war, international conventions, and he briefed us on all that so we could decide on further action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As regards a question concerning the Crisis Staff, we did not find in the transcript something that you said, which was that the ideas actually that there was a proclamation, a decision made to establish a Crisis Staff --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interlocutors be asked to slow down. We missed the last two interventions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are speaking too fast, both of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So the question was: Did you say today that the Crisis Staff became operational only upon the outbreak of the war?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have this, P6238. It's a telegram. Sorry. No. No. 00603, 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What page, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need 26. Page 26, line 12. Oh, there it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With respect, I still can't find in the transcript where the witness is to have said what Dr. Karadzic alleges he said and based this question on. So I'm wondering where we're going with this, especially as it doesn't seem to have arisen during the course of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't follow your comment, Ms. Edgerton. Mr. Karadzic now wants to see the SDS Bratunac minutes which you showed us.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. I was going back to Dr. Karadzic's question at page 62, line 5: "As regards a question concerning the Crisis Staff, we didn't find in the transcript something you said ..." A decision, which was that the idea was -- yeah. So I'm just -- and then Dr. Karadzic asked the witness to confirm: "Did you say today that the Crisis Staff only became operational on the outbreak of war," and the witness said, "That's what I said," and I can't find that anywhere in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that was the point of Mr. Karadzic's intervention. Could you help us, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In line 6, 62, it says: "We did not find it in the transcript." What I said was that it didn't make it into the transcript, and I couldn't intervene, although I turned on my mike. That is what was not recorded at the time when Mr. Djukanovic was talking about it. Now, I made a mistake -- no, let's stay with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is this a meeting of, the entire Municipal Board, the Presidency of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see, these are the minutes of the Presidency of the SDS Municipal Board in Bratunac. It was their meeting. It was a smaller body, not the entire board.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have P6237, my mistake. It's the same document, but then we need page 26.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we saw pages 55 and 56, and 66.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. Apologies. In the transcript it's page 26, line 12, where it is stated that it was the Municipal Assembly, and it was not the Municipal Assembly but the Presidency of the party. In any case, can we have the page where it is mentioned that the Crisis Staff was being formed, which is ERN number 021927 -- aha, the Serb version 9, the English 8. Yes. To the right, please. Not left, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At this session of the 25th of October, 1991, when you established the party Crisis Staff, did you establish it as per that or a -- an instruction of the 23rd of December or any kind of instruction of the Main Board?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: No. It was at our own initiative that we established it, Mr. President. When I say "at our own initiative," it may sound serious, but it was dictated by the situation because we were forced to gather and decide what to do. By the time different kinds of things started taking place such as the killings I have mentioned in my statement, there were all sorts of things. There was a rally at midnight, for example. People would set up demonstrations in Bratunac saying, "This is Bosnia, Serbs go to Serbia," and some such things. Our women took our children and fled across the Drina. These were difficult times, misfortunate times, but the staff was established and became operational officially when the real crisis broke out, which is what you said a moment ago did not make it into the transcript. By that time the paramilitaries had arrived and the war was underway.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In this document that was admitted, we can see you were a member. Can you tell us -- on page 17 you were asked about suspension. Were you the only one or were there more people who were suspended?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Together with me, I was one of 59 of those who were suspended. We were thrown out of the Main Board and People's Assembly. At the moment I was a deputy of the People's Assembly. And I was driven away from our work posts. It lasted all the way until 2011 when the sanctions were stopped by the current High Representative. I apologise, Mr. President, to go off on a tangent in explaining my answer, but given the fact that we were sanctioned by the OHR, I think it was a body of the world government -- of the Security Council of the UN, we expected to receive some kind of satisfaction from our state or from those who sanctioned us unjustly, but nothing of it followed. And even to date, since 2004, I have been in the same situation without work, as if I am still under this sanction, as if I were still supporting you back there as it was stated in that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 65 ter 24810, which is a decision by Lord Ashdown. Page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you receive the text of his decision and an explanation?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: That decision was delivered to me. There was an accompanying letter as well. He personally addressed each and every one of us, and there was another piece of paper that we received in which he says that he had to do what he did. He says in that that we were a member of a support network. We were portrayed as some sort of al-Qaeda. I don't know what the charges were against us exactly, but none of them were true, but there was no reference to anything that happened during the war. It was just you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You anticipated my next question. After the Dayton Accords, were you certified to participate in the elections and in the public political life?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was a candidate in the elections. I was elected an MP. I was a member of the Municipal Council. I was engaged in politics. I worked in the administration, and for a while I was the CO of an administrative organisation. I was engaged in sales in the public sector. However, after all those bans, all those rights were abolished, and what I personally knew and what I could do well was administration. I had spent a lot of time working in administration. I had a lot of experience. I was even deprived of that. And not only me but many of the other people who still had the same status as they had when Lord Ashdown made his decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Allow me to read this in English. It will be translated to you in Serbian. Paragraph 4: [In English] "For over a decade and throughout the war, the SDS has held the reins of political power in Republika Srpska. The entity's failure to apprehend those indicted individuals in flagrant disregard of Bosnia and Herzegovina's obligations under international law is, therefore, a damning indictment of SDS's commitment to proper governance. Given its dubious legacy as the political party founded by and initially presided over by the chief ICTY indictee at large, Radovan Karadzic, it was doubly incumbent upon SDS to effect expiation and rehabilitation by proactively pursuing and bringing to book the erstwhile architects of its dubious -- odious policies which so disfigured the polity. That it has not done so is a testament, at best, to its negligent abdication of governmental responsibility or, at worst, to its concerted will to obstruct peace implementation by clinging to vestiges (and figures) of its bankrupt past." [Interpretation] How did you understand this pearl of international justice and law? Did you receive that among the documents that you were provided with?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was part of the decision. What remains is just bitterness, as one would popularly say. I don't know what to say to that, how to react. We never obstructed the peace accords. We were not members of any support network. These words are wrong, and the way Lord Ashdown portrayed us, this is just wrong. However, he was the main interpreter of the Dayton Accords, and pursuant to the Bonn competencies that do not arise from the Dayton Accords, he was given some rights - I don't know who gave those rights to him - but he was entitled to punish us and remove us from the public life, to humiliate us before ourselves and before others. He took away our jobs, friends, and everything else. We want to take him to court in his country. We will try to find funds, although our situation is very dire, but from now on, this is going to be our main mission, to arrive at the truth and to find justice for ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And just one more question. On page 37, you were talking about a meeting, a meeting that took place on the 18th of October. Did Mr. Deronjic mention a meeting, or did he show you a telegram or some other document, or did he just verbally convey to you what he had brought from the Main Board?

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I already told you that I never received anything from you, either verbally or in writing. On that occasion I did not receive anything in writing either. Whatever is in the minutes, I already told you that I would attribute that to the agreement that he reached with the Prosecutor. To be honest, I'm not clear on anything in these minutes. Perhaps Deronjic just came up with it -- with that on top of his head. Maybe I don't have the right to say that, Mr. President. However, I cannot establish any links with that meeting and the minutes. And as for anything in writing and especially if we are talking about the A and B plan, I didn't know anything about that. I didn't see anything in writing. And the same goes for this Lukavac thing that Ms. Prosecutor showed me. I really didn't see anything of that kind arriving in Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Djukanovic, for having been a very good executive power. I am sorry for all your suffering. Unfortunately, I couldn't help you. And you are right as rain and still you suffered. Thank you for having testified here.

utterances.speaker: RODOLJUB DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to say good-bye to you and everybody else. And if I may add another sentence. I claim that I have told only the truth and that the diaries and all the other things are wrong. At one moment I felt like I had been accused here, especially based on the words that were used against me which were not only ugly but really pathetic and sad. So much from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That concludes your evidence. Thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go, Mr. Djukanovic. Given the time we'll take a break now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll resume at 1.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Micic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you commence your evidence, Mr. Micic, I must draw your attention to a certain Rule that we have here at the International Tribunal, that is, Rule 90(E) of Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Under this Rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecution, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that would amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question, but in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled in such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, Mr. Micic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Micic.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have two requests upon you. The first one is to make a long pause between my question and your answer, and the second is to speak slowly, approximately at this rate, although I cannot be a role model, because I often speak very fast. Please bear these two things in mind. If you're looking at the transcript in front of you, when the cursor stops and a capital letter A appears on the screen, that's your cue for starting answering. Did you provide my Defence team a statement?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D7972 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the screen before you, do you see that statement of yours?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: Yes, but can it be zoomed in a little, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this the statement that you provided?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is the statement that I provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you read the statement, and did you also sign it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is still too fast. Please make a longer pause. Is this your signature, sir?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this statement a true reflection of what you said to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions to you today, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that in essence they would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you have a hard copy of your statement in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: You mean on paper?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: No, I don't have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We will ask the Trial Chamber to be provided with a hard copy that you will be able to peruse if some paragraphs from it are mentioned in any of the questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender this statement into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3196, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no questions for this witness at this moment. My examination-in-chief is thus over. [In English] Ah, sorry, sorry. I forgot to read summary. [Interpretation] I'm now going to read a short summary of Mr. Dusan Micic's statement in English. [In English] Dusan Micic was born on 10th of March, 1960, in Slapasnica, Bratunac municipality. He was a military policeman in the Bratunac Territorial Defence from May 1992 to March 1993. Then he was the commander of the 3rd Platoon of the 1st Company of PJP, police formation. The military police was located in the old Vuk Karadzic primary school. One day when Mr. Dusan Micic passed by the school, he saw some soldiers whom he did not know taking people in and out of the school. He did not interfere, because they were in the JNA uniforms. He did not see anyone beating those people or that they were injured. His commander warned them on one -- or that no one should go to that school, otherwise would be dismissed from the police immediately. Another day Dusan Micic and his colleague were ordered to escort two buses of Muslims to Luke near Kladanj. They arrived at Luke until they reached the Muslim line and a check-point without soldiers. The people got off the bus -- buses and continued by foot. They stayed until those people left. Two days later, he heard that all the Muslims were driven away from the school to Pale one night. His police had nothing to do with that school while those Muslims were there. In July 1995, he and his unit gathered and were told that there was a large number of Muslims from Srebrenica in Potocari, and they were assigned to search the terrain from Zuti Most towards Potocari. He saw a crowd gathered in front of the factory, and when he passed by the crowd, he saw General Mladic giving food to the people. While in Potocari, neither Dusan Micic nor any of his men noticed that anyone was singled out from the crowd, beaten, or killed. One night in Sandici locality he heard shooting from the woods. When he woke up, he was informed that the Muslims had attacked and some of his men were wounded or seriously injured. On 12th of July, 1995, in Sandici, buses with Muslims, probably from Potocari, starting passing by. Dusan Micic did not remember if the buses were also passing on 13th of July, but probably not. That day, he went back to Bratunac. On his way, he saw a group of 50 to 60 Muslims on the pass in Sandici. When he passed by his colleagues -- passed by, his colleagues had told him that these people left the woods where the shooting came from and that they had surrendered. Those people were guarded by several soldiers who were unfamiliar to him. He did not know if they were policemen or from the army. Later in Bratunac, he saw buses and lorries with Muslims were passing through a side street where the Muslims had spent the night, towards Konjevic Polje. Regarding the killing of Muslims in Bratunac that night, Dusan Micic was not aware of anything at that time. He learned about it later but did not know how many were killed or who killed them. With regard to the incident in Kravica on 13th of July, 1995, he only learned about it later when the suspects were arrested. He did not know where the bodies were buried. And that is short summary. I do not questions for this witness for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Although the summary does not form part the witness's evidence, I have a question about it. You read, page 72, lines 20 to 23: "The military police was located in the old Vuk Karadzic primary school. One day when Mr. Dusan Micic passed by the school, he saw some soldiers." Are you referring to the same school building? You can clarify with the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many schools were there? Was that the same school, and what was the situation with the buildings?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: That was an old school that was disused. It was located not far away from the school where the Muslims were, maybe 100 or 150 metres, but it hadn't been used for at least ten years previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The one that you're talking about where the police was ceased to be a school ten years before the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: Yes, most probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But there is another school where the Muslims were?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: Well, that was one 100 or 150 metres from that school.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is a hangar part of it or is that a third facility?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: That's a third facility located behind the school and behind the gym.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The old or the new one?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: The new school, new school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours. Sorry, Mr. Karadzic. I don't mean to interrupt, but if Mr. Karadzic likes, we could find the aerial of Bratunac which shows the old school and the various buildings. Up to him and the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm satisfied with this, but it's up to the Prosecution to call the footage up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's leave it at that. Mr. Micic, as you have noted, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in writing, that is, through your written statement in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Micic.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I want to start by just asking you one thing about the PJP and your company. Your company, as you said in your statement to Dr. Karadzic's Defence counsel, was the first of the number of PJP companies in the Zvornik CJB. Now, the 1st Company is actually the elite company of the PJP, isn't it? You're kind of like their strike force?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: Well, you could say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay. Just -- now, His Honour Judge Kwon asked you about something that wasn't in your statement, and I want to ask you about something else that I didn't see in your Defence statement. Tell me if this is correct: In July 1995, you were guarding the prisoners when they were brought to the Vuk Karadzic school in Bratunac, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: No, you're not right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, now I'm puzzled about that for a couple of reasons. First of all, we got that information from the Defence. They have an obligation to tell us an outline in advance of what you're going to say, and on 26 February 2013, they gave us that outline. And it says here of you: "He also participated in guarding the prisoners in July 1995 when they were brought to the Vuk Karadzic school in Bratunac." So where does that come from?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: I have no idea about that statement, and I can guarantee to you and to this Court that I was never there at the time. It's a mistake. I couldn't have been there at the time, because I was busy elsewhere with other business.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But they must have got that from somewhere. Are you saying they made it up?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if they made that up. Anyway, it was impossible for me to be in or outside the school in 1995 when I had other commitments and duties, and I never did the guard duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Well, let's go through -- let's go through --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Pardon me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's go through the summary of what your evidence was expected to be, and you tell me what's correct in there, all right? The first sentence says you're a military policeman in the Bratunac Territorial Defence during 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You were a security guard in the Vuk Karadzic elementary school. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: No, it's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You will testify that paramilitaries were involved in the incident and not members of the TO. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: On 12 July 1995, your platoon was in the area of Potocari and Kravica. Correct or not?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And as Dr. Karadzic says in your summary, you will testify that there were no killings in Potocari while your platoon was there. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And your unit was not involved in the Kravica incident.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: What do you mean the Kravica incident? I don't know what you have in mind. Which incident?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm reading you the summary of your evidence. Is there an incident in Kravica you were involved in?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: My unit was not involved in any incident in Kravica that took place there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the last sentence that we've already talked about, you also participated -- it says: "He also participated in guarding the prisoners in July 1995 when they were brought to the Vuk Karadzic school in Bratunac." And you've said that that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I have reference, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The reference is the 65 ter filing of 26 February 19 -- pardon me, 2013.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: But there is a more fresh summary, 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But she's asking the witness about the summary she got. Probably you may clarify how come that sentence got into the summary, but otherwise your intervention is not appropriate, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] So there's two things --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry, that might be my voice or the way I'm standing.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: There's two things in your -- in this summary that you say are not accurate, and I want to go into one of those a little bit more and that's what happened in 1995. You must, since you've talked about 1995 in your statement, remember Danilo Zoljic. He was the commander of the Zvornik PJPs; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are you still in contact with him?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: Not at the moment. There's no need for that. I don't think that he still works for the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, he gave a statement to authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 2005, and perhaps we could have a look at that. 65 ter number 24857. And that's about the same subjects that you talked about in your Defence statement and your interrogation in 2008. So Mr. Zoljic to security authorities in Bijeljina in 2005 --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And perhaps we could go over to English page 5 and B/C/S page 3, at the very bottom of page 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So Mr. Zoljic, in 2005, talked about what the Zvornik PJPs were doing in July of 1995 as well, and he says halfway through page 5 in English and from the very bottom of page 3 in B/C/S and to the top of page 4, he says: "I also remember that there were cases involving the capture of their Muslim soldiers as well as male civilians who were then transported onto Bratunac by coach." He said: "I can't vouch for the exact date, but I think that it was during the night of 14 July 1995 when the 1st Company," that's your company, "and the Sekovici 2nd Detachment were pulled out of the line and deployed to the security detail for coaches transporting the prisoners and the security detail for the school in Bratunac." So Mr. Zoljic says that your company was doing exactly what is in your 65 ter summary, what the Defence towed us your evidence would be, isn't he? He says your company was involved in guarding captured soldiers and civilians in Bratunac. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page in Serbian, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Top of page -- top of page 4. So go to the next page in Serbian, very top.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you tell me the part in English? Where do we have it?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's not the correct page. If you could indulge me for a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's page 4, yes. Previous.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My apologies. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So I wonder if you could answer the question. Why does the commander of the Zvornik PJPs say that your company was guarding the prisoners in Bratunac? Which is exactly what we were told your evidence is going to be.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: I can say that this was his personal view. I was a member of the company, but my platoon and not all of it was involved. Only members of the Bratunac police station on the morning of the 13th were withdrawn from Konjevic Polje and Sandici to Bratunac in connection with the killing of Zeljko Ninkovic, a police officer from our police station. These are the men I'm talking about. As for the rest of my company, where they were deployed, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You're a platoon commander and you don't know where the rest of your company was deployed?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They remained behind when I left Konjevic Polje. They remained in Sandici where this tragedy happened, the killing of our colleague. And after that I didn't need to know about that. There were people higher up the chain who were supposed know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Something else that puzzles me about Zoljic's statement. He continues on this page, saying: "Captured soldiers and able-bodied civilians," and that's at the bottom of the page in English in front of us. "Captured soldiers and able-bodied civilians, there were around 2.500 to 3.000 of them were transported to Zvornik under our escort," so PJP escort, "and handed over and placed under the jurisdiction of the Zvornik Brigade." So that's something else that your units were involved in, and that's not in your statement either, is it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: Well, I can give you a similar answer. I don't know on which day did they participate in the escort to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Which company?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me the date and the day when the company was involved in escorting the captured Muslims to Zvornik? That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Were there so many convoys of Muslims being escorted to Zvornik that you need additional information to determine when it might have happened?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. I want to know the date so that I can tell you where I was when that was going on and only then can I give you an answer. Was that the 13th and the 14th?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It was the 13th -- it was the 13th at night, and the 14th during the day, when you said actually you had been to Bratunac where thousands of prisoners were already locked down in facilities in the town.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: May I answer? I don't know the number, whether there were thousands of them. On the 13th, I and members of the Bratunac police station left Sandici and we went to prepare the funeral of our colleague, and I was engaged with that the whole day. In Orthodoxy it takes a lot to prepare a funeral. You need to prepare food and drink. And he was a refugee from Zenica and he was a poor person. So I didn't know what was going on. And I'm talking only about members of the Bratunac police station. I don't know about others. And the same applies to the 14th. The funeral took place on the 14th. We spent the whole day at the deceased's house, and we buried him eventually. So I never even passed through that area on that day. And as for what Danilo Zoljic is talking about, it's his problem. I don't know. I never saw those men on the 13th and the 14th, members of my unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: There's something else that actually doesn't add up, to my mind, from some of the statements you've previously given. Now, in your statement to Dr. Karadzic's Defence, you referred to your interrogation by the Bosnia-Herzegovina prosecutor's office in 2008, and we can have a look at that to refresh your memory. It's 65 ter number 24855. You recognise the statement you gave in 2008?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's go over to page 6, I think in both languages, paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And this is about your duties on the 12th of July in Potocari. And you're --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, indulge me, please, again for a moment with respect to the English language pages. Page 9 in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you said, with respect to your duties on the 12th of July, that Commander Pantic explained to you that you were searching the terrain on the right side of the road in order to take over that terrain to prevent the paramilitary formations on the side of the Serb forces from attacking the Muslim population gathered in Potocari. Is that true? Is it your evidence that you were searching for Serb paramilitary forces?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: We were not searching. We were scouring the terrain in order to ensure security for the Muslims gathered there, to prevent any incident or attacks on them. That's why we were searching the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: By who? Incidents or attacks by who?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: Possibly by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So let me get this straight. On the 12th of July, PJP units -- 12th of July, 1995, PJP units, VRS units, in large numbers, units from Jahorina and others descend on Potocari to surround Potocari and to take control of Potocari, and your evidence is that your task is to protect the Muslims and secure them from attack by Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have the reference to take control of Potocari. Where can we find this? Line 8.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do Your Honours want me to list the names of the DutchBat soldiers who came to testify in these proceedings about this incident? I don't know what Dr. Karadzic is asking for here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: It might be easier -- I noticed that the witness was almost about to answer your question, so it might be easier if he does that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you want me to repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: I'll try to answer. The units you cited, some from Sarajevo and from elsewhere, at the time I was up there with my unit, there was -- there were no such units there. I didn't see a single one for as long as I was there with my unit. I don't know what happened after I left. I was there for two or three hours with my unit, and then we withdrew to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My question was about your task. You stand by your assertion in 2008 that your task was to protect the Muslims and secure them from attack by Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: Yes. I stand by it even now. I'm very proud of it. We were successful in doing that. During my unit's stay up there, there was not a single incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I want to show you another document from somebody else that you would know from that time. It's Dragomir Vasic. Now, he was the chief of the Zvornik CJB, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So he's your boss.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: He was the head of the centre, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to show you what he said your job was.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have a look at P2996, please. And it's a report to the minister of the interior from Vasic. On 12 July 1992. And you're going to have to magnify the Serbian version. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So have a look at this document, line 6. Dragomir Vasic, your chief, talks about joint police forces advancing on Potocari with the aim of taking UNPROFOR personnel prisoner, surrounding the entire civilian population, and cleaning the terrain of enemy groups. So your boss says that your job was something completely different from what you say it was. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic was my boss, but my boss at the time was Radomir Pantic, and I received my tasks from him. I didn't see Vasic at all that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So are you saying that Vasic -- Vasic isn't telling the truth when he writes this document?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: It's not what I'm saying. I am simply don't want to get involved in this. He was my chief, and it's up to him what he wants to write down. I'm only telling you about where I was and what I did together with my unit. I received my tasks from Radomir Pantic directly and not from Vasic. I received orders from him.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Let's go back to your statement in 2008, 65 ter number 24855. And let's go over to paragraph 11. And that's at pages 11 of the English translation and 11 of the B/C/S, I hope. In -- in this statement that you gave in 2008, you talked about your unit's deployment to Sandici on the evening of the 12th, and there you stated that Pantic, who you've just talked about, told you that at Sandici you can't allow anyone to stop the vehicles with the civilians coming from Potocari and that you had to provide those vehicles pass undisturbed. And then further in that same document you said: "I haven't had information on the evening of 12 July that male Muslims, armed soldiers, were moving through the forest." So was that true when you said that in 2008?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: I don't know when. It depends when I learned of it. I don't recall it. When could I have learned that they could go through the forest?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's your statement, so these are your words. One would think you would know. My question to you was: Is this true, what I just read to you from your statement in 2008?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we at least have the entire sentence read out, if not the passage, the sentence to the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Did you find the sentence, Mr. Micic, and read it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the middle, Sekovici, and then further in the text.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "That evening I noticed a single tank." Is that it, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The next evening."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "I noticed the crew, and later I learned that the tank" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not understand the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Just a second. Why don't we give it another try. Could you let the witness know the sentence. Where is it, Ms. Edgerton, in the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness found it, but he was reading fast.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do it slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You don't have to read out. Read it and then answer the question. Let us know when your reading is done, Mr. Micic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only the part pertaining to the forest. The rest you don't need to read, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do I need to read it out or do you want me to respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, that's fine --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Read it to yourself and then answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And what was your question, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My question was whether what he said about the orders from Commander Pantic was true.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is true. It's just that in the evening upon arrival I had no information. During the night and later, I learned more. I learned that during the night there was some movement of units, but in the evening when we were deployed along the line and the road we had no information. At least I didn't. That's what he conveyed to me. During the night we already received some information. We were there the whole night, from dusk 'til dawn.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the information that you received was that a column of thousands of Bosnian Muslim boys and men was trying to escape from Srebrenica, and your task was to block them, and capture them, and eliminate them. That's what you were doing at Sandici. Wasn't that your job? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: Well, that was never a task. One cannot discuss it at all. If we had done that we would have, but what else? What about those we escorted and secured?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, let's look at another document from your boss, Vasic. It's P4937. 4937. So this is another document from your boss on the 12th of July, 1995, to the minister of the interior, where he says 8.000 men, about 1500 of whom are armed, are in the Konjevic Polje and Sandici sector, and the Sekovici Special Detachment and the 1st Company of the PJP, that's your company, are blocking this section with the goal of destroying these forces. So here's another document where Vasic says your job is something other than what you say it is. So is Vasic lying?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: I can't say that he's lying, but I can't get involved in what Vasic stated. It's up to him how he viewed the situation. My view was different, and it was in light of what we were doing in the field. And it was proven that in the field where my unit was there were no killings. [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I find it interesting that you don't want to get involved in it, because in fact, Mr. Micic, everybody knew what was going on at Sandici, and, for example, Dr. Karadzic himself received a report from General Miletic on 12 July 1995 - and the reference is P3054 - about events in the area. Dr. Karadzic even read or even received information that said during the day, Potocari was liberated, Serb forces continued to advance in order to liberate all the settlements in the Srebrenica enclave, part of our units and MUP units have organised ambushes in order to break out from the enclave towards Tuzla. So it's not only the chief of the CJB but the VRS Main Staff was reporting up to Karadzic what was going on, and your evidence is your unit had nothing to do there. You slept through it effectively is what you said in your statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I was tired that night. When I was in the field, I deployed my men, established communication and withdrew some 30 to 50 metres away from them, and I fell asleep. I was asleep when the shooting occurred.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you slept through. You heard no shots. You saw no Muslims being surrendered -- surrendering. You saw no Muslims being captured the whole time you were on the line at Sandici. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: I assert -- well, I haven't slept through it, but I've slept from perhaps 10 to 15 minutes. But at the time during the night, no Muslims were surrendering on the 13th in the morning. That is to say, the night between the 12th and the 13th. There -- people were not surrendering that night while I was there. On the 13th, in agreement with my commanders, I went to Bratunac to inquire about the situation with my colleague. They told me to go to the base, and then I would be informed. When I arrived in Bratunac, when I entered the police station, they told me that Zeljko Ninkovic had died. I immediately went to see the chief --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry, Zeljko Ninkovic was also a member of the 1st Company of the PJP, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Because you didn't say that in your statement. Because you didn't say that in your statement either.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I didn't? Well, no one asked me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Micic, by the 13th of July, Serb forces had captured or received around 1.500 Muslim soldiers who were making their way through the very meadow where your unit, your company, and your platoon was situated, and your evidence is it didn't happen while you were there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: Yes. If you allowed me, I will tell you where I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
